ex-E202-1.title: Path of an α particle
ex-E202-1.question:
An α particle is directed to a thin gold foil. It is deflected by a gold nucleus and moves along the path as shown. The position of the gold nucleus is not shown in the figure.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

(1) The gold nucleus is in region A.

(2) The change in momentum of the α particle will be very small if it collides with an electron, instead of the gold nucleus.

(3) The KE of the α particle is at a minimum when it is closest to the gold nucleus.

A (1) only

B (2) only

C (1) and (3) only

D (2) and (3) only
ex-E202-1.answer:
From the path, it can be inferred that the repulsive electric force acting on the α particle points towards region A. Therefore, the gold nucleus should be in region B.

∴ (1) is incorrect.

The mass of an α particle is much larger than that of an electron, so its change in momentum is very small when colliding with an electron.

∴ (2) is correct.

When the α particle approaches the gold nucleus, its KE is converted into the electric potential energy between it and the nucleus. When it is closest to the gold nucleus, the electric potential energy is at a maximum and the KE is at a minimum.

∴ (3) is correct.

∴ The answer is D.
ex-E202-1.location: Book E2  |  Chapter E202  |  Source PDF p. 5

ex-E202-2.title: Line spectra
ex-E202-2.question:
The emission spectra for hydrogen, helium and carbon are shown below.

The emission spectrum of an unknown sample A and the absorption spectrum of another unknown sample B are shown below.

(a) Determine the element composition of samples A and B.

(b) What evidence about the energy of an atom does a line spectrum provide?
ex-E202-2.answer:
(a) Sample A is composed of hydrogen and helium as the spectral lines of these elements can be found in the emission spectrum of sample A.

Sample B is composed of carbon as the spectral lines of this element can be found in the absorption spectrum of sample B.

(b) The energy of an atom can only take certain discrete values.

ex-E202-3.title: Bohr orbit
ex-E202-3.question:
According to Bohr’s model, the radius of the innermost orbit of the electron in a hydrogen atom is 5.29 × 10–11 m.

(a) Find the radius of the electron’s orbit corresponding to quantum

number n = 2.

(b) If the electron moves to an orbit corresponding to a larger n, how will its speed change?
ex-E202-3.answer:
(a) By rn = n2r1,

r2 = (2)2(5.29 × 10–11) = 2.12 × 10–10 m

(b) By mevnrn = nh2π and rn = n2r1,

vn = nh2πmern = nh2πme(n2r1) = h2πmenr1 ∝ 1n

If n becomes larger, the speed vn will become smaller.

ex-E202-4.title: Raising an electron to higher energy states
ex-E202-4.question:
Consider Bohr’s model of the hydrogen atom. The ground state energy of the electron is −13.6 eV.

(a) State the physical significance of energy levels having negative values.

(b) Find the excitation energy required to raise the electron from the

ground state to the first excited state (n = 2).

(c) Can the electron in the ground state absorb a photon of energy 10.3 eV?

(d) Find the energy required for the electron to jump from the first excited state to the second excited state.
ex-E202-4.answer:
(a) The negative values of energy levels mean that the electron is bound by the nucleus.

(b) Excitation energy = E2 – E1 = (–13.622) – (–13.6)= 10.2 eV

(c) No

(d) Energy required = E3 – E2 = (–13.632) – (–13.622) = 1.89 eV
ex-E202-4.tips:
Tip

To raise an electron to a higher energy state, the energy of the photon must be exactly the same as the energy difference between the two states.
ex-E202-4.think: Will the energy required for the electron to jump from the second excited state to the third excited state be larger or smaller than the answer in (d)?
ex-E202-4.thinkAnswer: Smaller. The second and third excited states have n=3 and n=4. Using En=−13.6n2 eV, Δ E=E4−E3=13.6(132−142)=0.661 eV. This is less than 1.89 eV in (d), because adjacent levels become closer together as n increases.
ex-E202-4.location: Book E2  |  Chapter E202  |  Source PDF p. 24

ex-E202-5.question:

All possible transitions are as shown.

Transition

Energy released

n = 3 to n = 2

(−1.51) − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV

ex-E202-6.title: Ionizing a hydrogen atom
ex-E202-6.question:
The ground state energy of a hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV.

(a) Find the ionization energy of a hydrogen atom.

(b) A hydrogen atom is in an excited state. Is the minimum energy needed to ionize it higher or lower than the ionization energy?

(c) A hydrogen atom is in the first excited state. Can it absorb a photon of energy 10 eV? Explain.
ex-E202-6.answer:
(a) Ionization energy = E∞ – E1 = 0 – (–13.6) = 13.6 eV

(b) Lower

(c) Minimum energy to ionize the atom = E∞ – E2 = 0 – (– 13.622) = 3.4 eV

Since the photon energy is higher than 3.4 eV, the atom can absorb the photon and become ionized.
ex-E202-6.tips:
Tip

An atom in an excited state has higher energy, so less energy is needed to ionize it.
ex-E202-6.location: Book E2  |  Chapter E202  |  Source PDF p. 27

ex-E202-8.title: Excitation by electron and photon
ex-E202-8.question:
The figure shows some energy levels of a hydrogen atom.

Determine whether a hydrogen atom in the ground state can be excited by each of the following particles, and to which state it can be excited to.

(a) An electron of kinetic energy 10.0 eV

(b) An electron of kinetic energy 12.2 eV

(c) A photon of energy 12.2 eV
ex-E202-8.answer:
From n = 1 to n = 2, ΔE = –3.40 – (–13.6) = 10.2 eV

From n = 1 to n = 3, ΔE = –1.51 – (–13.6) = 12.09 eV

From n = 1 to n = 4, ΔE = –0.85 – (–13.6) = 12.75 eV

(a) As 10.0 eV is smaller than 10.2 eV, the atom cannot be excited.

(b) As 12.2 eV is larger than 10.2 eV and 12.09 eV, the atom can be

excited to either the first excited state (n = 2) or the second excited state

(n = 3).

(c) The energy of the photon is not equal to the excitation energy, so the atom cannot be excited.
ex-E202-8.location: Book E2  |  Chapter E202  |  Source PDF p. 32

ex-E202-10.title: Wavelengths of moving objects
ex-E202-10.question:
(a) Find the de Broglie wavelengths of

(i) a tennis ball of mass 50 g moving at 60 m s–1,

(ii) an electron of mass 9.11 × 10–31 kg moving at 5 × 106 m s–1.

(b) How will the de Broglie wavelength of an object change if its speed increases?
ex-E202-10.answer:
(a) (i) λ = hmv = 6.63 × 10–34(0.05)(60) = 2.21 × 10–34 m

(ii) λ = hmv = 6.63 × 10–34(9.11 × 10–31)(5 × 106) = 1.46 × 10–10 m

(b) According to λ = hmv, λ will decrease if v increases.
ex-E202-10.think: What would the speed of a tennis ball be if its de Broglie wavelength is 1 m? How long would the ball take to move 1 cm? Can we observe the wave nature of the tennis ball?
ex-E202-10.thinkAnswer:
Using the given mass of 0.05 kg, v=hmλ=6.63×10−340.05×1=1.33×10−32 m s−1.

To move 1 cm, t=sv=0.011.326×10−32=7.54×1029 s, about 2.39×1022 years.

The required speed is effectively zero on laboratory scales, so wave behaviour of the tennis ball is not observable in this proposed experiment. At ordinary speeds its de Broglie wavelength is far too small for observable diffraction.
